china.name: Xiangyang preserved mustard root (datoucai)
china.place: Xiangyang, Hubei
china.materials: Root mustard, salt, and seasonings that vary by product.
china.process: Repeated salting, brining, sun-drying and sealed maturation are traditionally summarized as “three saltings, five brinings and six dryings.” Fermentation, salt penetration and dehydration together create its flavor and texture.
china.taste: Salty and savory with a little sweetness; its matured flavor differs from the sharp pungency of fresh mustard root. Seasoned versions vary.
china.eat: Shredded and dressed as a small side dish; Stir-fried with shredded pork; Braised or steamed with pork belly.

china.name: Northeastern Sour Napa Cabbage (Dongbei Suancai)
china.place: Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang, with related sour-cabbage traditions in northern Hebei and elsewhere in northern China.
china.materials: Napa cabbage, often long-headed local varieties; water and salt form the traditional fermentation medium. Household methods vary.
china.process: Whole cabbages or large pieces are packed into a crock, weighted and kept submerged to ferment. Some traditions use raw cabbage; others blanch it first. Fermentation creates the sourness, but there is no single recipe shared by every household.
china.taste: Clean cabbage sourness, salt and vegetable flavor; the traditional basic version does not depend on a chili paste.
china.eat: Pork belly poached or stewed with sour cabbage; Sour cabbage, pork and blood sausage, often called shazhu cai; Sour cabbage with glass noodles or frozen tofu; Sour-cabbage hotpot; Pork-and-sour-cabbage dumplings or steamed buns.

china.name: Hetao Sour Cabbage
china.place: Bayannur and the Hetao region of Inner Mongolia.
china.materials: Cabbage varieties described locally as qingmaye, pingtoubai and juanxinbai.
china.process: Local descriptions layer cabbage and salt in a crock and add weights. Liquid released by the vegetables creates the fermentation environment, unlike some cabbage traditions that begin with added brine. This is a description of the tradition rather than a household recipe.
china.taste: Sour, salty and cabbage-rich. In the finished stew, its acidity joins the richness of pork and fat.
china.eat: Pork-and-sour-cabbage stew; Sour cabbage stewed with potatoes; Hetao mixed stew with tofu and glass noodles; Pork-and-sour-cabbage stew served with drained broomcorn-millet rice.

china.name: Korean-Chinese Spicy Napa Cabbage
china.place: Yanbian in Jilin, and Korean communities in Liaoning, Heilongjiang and other parts of northeastern China.
china.materials: Napa cabbage with chili, garlic, ginger and other seasonings; some local and household recipes include fish-based sauces.
china.process: Cabbage is first salted, then coated between the leaves with a prepared seasoning mixture and stored to ferment. The defining sequence joins salting, seasoning paste and further fermentation, rather than simply submerging cabbage in plain brine.
china.taste: A combination of chili heat, salt, sourness and often sweetness and savory depth. Acidity changes with ripeness and recipe.
china.eat: A small side dish with a meal; Soups and fried rice made with the fermented cabbage; specific recipes vary locally.

china.name: Korean-Chinese Cubed Radish Pickles
china.place: Rongxing in Panjin, Liaoning, and Korean communities across northeastern China.
china.materials: Radish cut into pieces; seasonings vary by place and household, with red-chili versions common.
china.process: Radish replaces cabbage as the main vegetable and is salted, seasoned and fermented. Cutting style and seasoning should be described for the particular local version.
china.taste: Typical red-chili versions are salty, sour and hot while retaining radish flavor. Not every version has the same level of heat.
china.eat: A small side dish with rice and everyday meals.

china.name: Tianshui Jiangshui Greens
china.place: Tianshui and Qin'an in Gansu, with related jiangshui traditions in Longnan.
china.materials: Seasonal bitter greens, celery, cabbage, shepherd's purse or radish tops, together with flour-based cooking liquid and an established fermentation starter.
china.process: Vegetables are cleaned, cut and blanched, then fermented with a flour-based liquid and starter. The starchy liquid and the continued use of previous jiangshui distinguish this family from ordinary seasoned-brine pickles.
china.taste: Refreshing acidity, from gently sour to distinctly tart. Noodle dishes may add chili oil, chives and other seasonings.

china.name: Hanzhong Jiangshui Greens

china.materials: Leafy mustard, locally called hualacai, and other greens; cabbage or celery may also be used. The medium includes established jiangshui or flour-based liquid.
china.process: Washed, blanched leaves undergo lactic fermentation in jiangshui or flour-based liquid. A Hanzhong local standard describes the greens as a semi-finished sour vegetable, often subsequently stir-fried, seasoned with hot oil or added to a staple dish.
china.taste: Sour and vegetal; jiangshui noodles commonly add chili oil and garlic shoots for an aromatic sour-hot dish.

china.place: Ziyang County in Ankang, Shaanxi, including Huangu and Shuang'an.

china.process: Local greens are sorted, washed, pickled and naturally fermented. Household methods and modern standardized products should be described separately; promotional accounts do not establish a universal salt level or fermentation time.
china.taste: Bright sourness and vegetable flavor, often with a golden-yellow appearance; acidity and saltiness differ between products.

china.name: Sichuan and Chongqing brine pickles (paocai)
china.place: Sichuan and Chongqing; widely made both at home and commercially
china.materials: Vegetables such as radish, cabbage, yardlong beans, cucumber and mustard greens; brine, with ginger, chilies, Sichuan pepper and other seasonings varying by household.
china.process: Vegetables are submerged in seasoned brine and undergo lactic acid fermentation in a closed vessel. Some households maintain and reuse an established brine. This is a continuing practice, not one fixed recipe shared by every jar.
china.taste: A sour and salty base, with heat, numbing spice and sweetness depending on the seasonings.

A home seafood meal in which xianji enhances yellow-croaker soup; rice-cake soup can become a complete one-bowl meal.

china.name: Fermented Amaranth Stalks (Mei Xiancai Geng)
china.place: Shaoxing and Ningbo in Zhejiang.
china.materials: Thick, mature stalks of the locally used amaranth-type plant; salt. Some methods use an established fermentation brine.
china.process: The stalks are cut, soaked, salted and matured in a jar. Local versions differ in whether the material is pre-cooked and whether old brine is used. The finished stalks are usually steamed before eating.
china.taste: Salty, savory and intensely fermented, contrasting with plain rice.
china.eat: Steamed fermented stalks finished with sesame oil; Steamed or cooked with tofu, pumpkin, taro or small fish.

china.fermentation: A local fermented vegetable. The traditional name does not establish that a single mold species drives the process.
china.scopeNote: Local plant names vary. The botanical identity should be confirmed for the specific place; ordinary market red-amaranth stalks are not assumed to be interchangeable.
china.texture: The outer stalk keeps its tube-like shape while the center can become soft, slippery and jelly-like; diners often suck out the tender core.
china.aroma: A powerful, distinctive pungent fermentation aroma.
variants: Shaoxing and Ningbo names, pre-treatment and brine use vary

A tasting focused on how a food's strong aroma differs from its texture and flavor.

china.name: Ningbo Pungent Fermented Winter Melon
china.place: Ningbo and the Ningbo-Shaoxing plain in Zhejiang.
china.materials: Winter melon, salt and an established pungent fermentation brine in the traditional version.
china.process: Cut winter melon is salted and, in traditional versions, matured in an established pungent brine. Both raw-pickled and pre-cooked routes exist. Mild, briefly salted refrigerated melon should not be equated with long-matured brine versions.
china.taste: Salty and savory, sometimes mildly sour. The naturally mild melon takes on the flavor of its brine.
china.eat: A small portion dressed with sesame oil and served with rice; Steamed according to the local preparation or product instructions.

A small hometown-flavor side dish at a family meal after returning home.

china.name: Ningbo Pungent Fermented Taro Stalks
china.place: Ningbo, Zhejiang.
china.materials: The above-ground leaf stalks of the locally used taro, rather than its underground corm; salt and established pungent brine.
china.process: One of Ningbo's three pungent vegetable specialties. Taro stalks are prepared, salted and matured in pungent brine. Household pre-cooking and brine methods differ.
china.taste: Salty and savory, with a pronounced fermented character.
china.eat: A small rice accompaniment; any further steaming or cooking should follow reliable local or product guidance.

china.scopeNote: This is not fermented taro corm. The edible plant and its preparation must be identified accurately; this entry does not provide a raw-eating or household-making recipe. Detailed sensory descriptions are less well documented than for the other two specialties.
china.texture: Soft stalk segments after maturation, with firmness depending on the raw material and preparation.
china.aroma: A brine aroma related to pungent winter melon and amaranth stalks, expressed through a different vegetable texture.
variants: Several local written forms name the stalk; they belong under one entry

occasions.text: A traditional side dish in Ningbo homes and small restaurants. Late summer and early autumn also bring the seasonal ingredients for the three pungent specialties.

china.name: Xiaoshan Dried Radish (Luobogan)
china.place: Xiaoshan in Hangzhou, Zhejiang, including Guali.
china.materials: Radish, traditionally the suitable yidaozhong variety, and salt.
china.process: Skin-on strips alternate between drying, salting and pressing in crocks before sealed maturation. The traditional description is three dryings and three saltings. Craft interviews describe this alternating process as staged maturation or fermentation.
china.taste: Salty and savory with natural sweetness; modern versions may add chili seasoning.
china.eat: Dried radish scrambled with eggs; Dried radish stir-fried with edamame; Dried radish with cured pork; Sweet-and-sour seasoned dried radish.

china.scopeNote: Winter production does not mean it is eaten only in winter. Historical medicinal or heat-protection claims are not treated as established health effects.
china.texture: Fairly even, fleshy strips combine the chew of a dried vegetable with a tender crunch.
china.aroma: A concentrated, matured dried-radish aroma.
variants: Plain and modern chili-seasoned products
Air-dehydrated and salt-dehydrated production routes

A little chopped radish in a lunchbox to add chew and crunch.

china.name: Yuyao Preserved Mustard Stem (Zhacai)
china.place: Yuyao on the southern shore of Hangzhou Bay, especially its northwestern coastal plain in Zhejiang.
china.materials: The swollen, knobbly stem of stem mustard, plus salt; finished products may receive further seasoning.
china.process: Trimmed mustard stems are salted to remove water, re-salted and matured, then sold whole, sliced or shredded. This belongs to the same broad zhacai family as Fuling, with its own growing area, suitable varieties and Zhejiang processing tradition.
china.taste: Salty and savory, often emphasizing freshness, tenderness and crunch. Seasoned versions vary widely and are not uniformly mild.
china.eat: Shreds stir-fried with pork; An ingredient in noodle soup; A little beside congee; these are general zhacai serving suggestions rather than rituals unique to Yuyao.

china.scopeNote: Compare Yuyao and Fuling through place, plant varieties, methods and product characteristics, without inventing a flavor ranking or a fixed salt difference. Inaccurate planting-season claims found in some reporting are not repeated.
china.texture: Thick, crunchy stem flesh; a whole stem and fine shreds provide different bites.
china.aroma: Matured mustard aroma, with additional notes reflecting any later seasonings.
variants: Whole, initially processed stems and ready-to-eat seasoned slices or shreds
A regional branch alongside Fuling within the zhacai family

occasions.text: A quick home meal, noodle soup or small breakfast side.

china.name: Tianjin Garlic-Scented Preserved Cabbage (Dongcai)
china.place: Jinghai District in Tianjin, including Chenguantun.
china.materials: Napa-cabbage leaves, salt and garlic; local and commercial recipes may use other seasonings.
china.process: Cabbage is selected, cut and dried to remove moisture, then mixed with salt and garlic and packed into jars to ferment and mature. It is a finely chopped, garlic-scented seasoning vegetable, distinct from Sichuan's Nanchong dongcai.
china.taste: Intensely salty-savory with clear garlic flavor; a small amount adds depth to soup.
china.eat: Wonton soup with dongcai; Noodle soup finished with dongcai; A small addition to stews or home-style stir-fries.

china.scopeNote: Dongcai names different foods in different places, so Tianjin and Nanchong retain separate regional entries. Traditional dongcai products are not assumed to contain live lactic acid bacteria.
china.texture: Finely chopped, tender-crisp and slightly chewy from dehydration, sometimes golden-yellow.
china.aroma: Garlic and mature fermented-vegetable aromas.
variants: The Chenguantun local tradition
Five-spice product names should be checked against their actual seasonings

occasions.text: An everyday Tianjin breakfast and snack-soup ingredient, including wonton and noodle soups.
Winter home stews and stir-fries; Tianjin Library introduces it in a seasonal account for Minor Cold.

china.name: Inverted-Jar Mustard Greens (Daoducai)
china.place: Jiande, Hangzhou and the sandy Qiantang plain in Zhejiang.
china.materials: Local mustard greens, including jiutoujie and broad-leaf varieties, and salt.
china.process: Mustard is washed, wilted and allowed to yellow, then chopped, rubbed with salt and pressed to remove liquid. It is tightly packed with a wooden stick into a jar, which is turned upside down for low-moisture fermentation. The inverted jar is its most recognizable process feature.
china.taste: Savory, salty and mellow, retaining mustard character. Acidity varies with maturation.
china.eat: Daoducai stir-fried with spring bamboo shoots; Daoducai with edamame or chili; An ingredient used by some Hangzhou pian'erchuan noodle shops; Steamed dishes or soups.

china.texture: Fine, supple pieces, with some crunch remaining in the stems.
china.aroma: Concentrated vegetable fragrance and mature jar-aged notes.
variants: Local mustard-variety names differ between producing areas
Some contemporary recipes add sliced preserved mustard root

Summer home cooking with edamame, steamed dishes or soup; noodle shops may switch between xuecai and daoducai according to availability.

china.name: Yangzhou Sauce-Pickled Vegetables (Jiangcai)
china.place: Yangzhou, Jiangsu.
china.materials: Vegetables such as baby cucumbers, crosnes, small radishes and tender ginger; salt and fermented sauce. Recipes depend on the product.
china.process: Vegetables are selected, trimmed and initially pickled, then matured in sauce to develop a salty-sweet, fermented-sauce flavor. The use of fermented sauce alone does not prove that each vegetable itself undergoes lactic fermentation.
china.taste: Fresh, sweet, crisp and tender, with balanced salt and sweetness rather than strong acidity.
china.eat: Sauce-pickled baby cucumber; Sauce-pickled crosnes; Mixed sauce pickles; Sweet-sauce melon or cucumber.

china.name: Beijing Traditional Sauce Pickles
china.place: Beijing.
china.materials: Cucumber, kohlrabi and other vegetables; salt; sweet wheat paste or soybean sauce.
china.process: Vegetables are first salted, then desalted and cut into shreds, chunks or strips as needed. In the traditional craft, small cloth bags of vegetables are immersed in specially prepared sweet wheat or soybean sauce and turned to absorb flavor evenly.
china.taste: Rich sauce flavor with sweetness and savory depth; the salt-sugar balance varies by variety.
china.eat: Maren jinsi, sesame-coated fine kohlrabi shreds; Small cucumbers in sweet sauce; Sweet-sauce cucumber strips finished with hot oil.

china.scopeNote: Sauce aroma is not the same as sourness, and fermentation of a sauce is not proof of fermentation of its vegetables. A brand's entire range should not be treated as one fixed recipe.
china.texture: Tender-crisp, in forms including fine shreds, cucumber strips and small whole cucumbers.
china.aroma: Mellow sweet-wheat-paste or soybean-sauce aroma.
variants: Different vegetables and cuts form product variants

A breakfast side with congee or steamed buns.

china.name: Hangzhou Sauce-Pickled Cucumber (Shuangchagua)
china.place: Hangzhou, Zhejiang; Jingyangguan is a representative producer.
china.materials: Cucumber, salt and a sauce-pickling medium.
china.process: Fresh cucumbers are salted to remove water, then placed in sauce crocks. The name is associated with two traditional salting stages. This Hangzhou specialty should not be equated with naturally lactic-fermented brine cucumbers.
china.taste: Pleasantly salty-sweet, with sauce complementing the cucumber.
china.eat: A small dish of shuangchagua beside paofan rice.

china.place: Chaoshan, Guangdong, including the traditions of Chenghai and Waisha in Shantou.
china.materials: Mustard greens, locally called dacai, and salt.
china.process: The greens are wilted in the sun, salted, packed down and fermented. Finished greens may be rinsed to reduce their saltiness before cutting. This specific mustard-green tradition differs from Sichuan paocai, where several vegetables may share an established brine.
china.taste: Sour and salty, sometimes with a gently sweet finish.
china.eat: Chopped greens with plain rice porridge; Pork-stomach soup with xiancai; Fish braised with xiancai, or fish soup.

china.aroma: A rounded, sour aroma of preserved mustard greens.

china.name: Chaoshan Olive and Mustard-Green Relish (Ganlancai)
china.place: Chaoshan, Guangdong, including Longhu and Chenghai in Shantou.
china.materials: Mustard greens, Chinese olives, vegetable oil and salt; some products include additional spices.
china.process: Traditional production can begin by salt-fermenting mustard greens. The greens are then desalted, chopped and drained, before being slowly cooked with prepared Chinese olives and oil. The finished product is a cooked, oil-rich relish.
china.taste: Salty, savory and concentrated, combining olive and mustard-green flavors.
china.eat: A spoonful alongside rice porridge or steamed rice; A seasoning for fried rice, steamed meat or vegetables in modern cooking.

china.name: Huizhou Preserved Mustard Greens (Meicai)
china.place: Huizhou, Guangdong; Hengli and Aipi in Huicheng are representative production areas.
china.materials: Large-leaf mustard greens and salt; sugar is added for sweet meicai.
china.process: Traditional production combines dry salting with sun-drying, piled maturation and final preparation. Sweet and salted versions are distinguished by added sugar. Despite the name, it contains no plums and is not automatically identical to fully dried Zhejiang meigancai.
china.taste: Salty and deeply savory; sweet meicai has an additional sweetness.

china.name: Hakka Sour Mustard Greens (Taiwan Tradition)

china.process: Sun-wilted greens are rubbed with salt to release liquid, packed firmly and fermented. This is the wetter stage in a related mustard-green preservation sequence; further dehydration and maturation can produce fucai and meigancai.

china.place: Hakka communities in Taiwan, including the mustard-green preservation traditions of Miaoli.

china.name: Chaoshan Preserved Radish and Aged Radish (Caipu)
china.place: Chaoshan, Guangdong, including Chenghai. Hakka communities also preserve radish, and those traditions are best compared as regional branches.
china.materials: White radish and salt; some aged-radish methods include spices.
china.process: The radish is salted, repeatedly sun-dried and pressed, then stored in earthenware containers. Long-matured forms are called lao caipu. Traditional storage can include fermentation, but simple salt-dried radish is not automatically the same ferment.
china.taste: Younger caipu is salty with a gentle sweetness; aged caipu is more concentrated.
china.eat: Caipu with plain rice porridge; Caipu omelet; Clay-pot porridge with aged caipu; Aged caipu in fish or meat soup.

china.name: Guangxi Sour Bamboo Shoots (Suansun)
china.place: Several parts of Guangxi, especially their use in Liuzhou luosifen and Nanning laoyoufen. Other provinces also ferment bamboo shoots.
china.materials: Bamboo shoots, with species varying by locality, and water; some processes use brine or a fermentation starter.
china.process: Whole, sliced or shredded shoots ferment and acidify in water or brine. Spontaneous and inoculated processes coexist. This is more than simply immersing shoots in vinegar.
china.taste: Sour and savory, with a pronounced bamboo-shoot character.

world.materials: Shredded cabbage, carrot, onion, hot peppers and vinegar
world.process: This crunchy, sour and hot condiment is commonly preserved with added vinegar rather than vegetable lactic fermentation. Included as a neighbouring pickle tradition, not a core fermented-vegetable entry.
world.eat: Alongside griot, fried chicken or fish, and fried plantain.

world.name: Gari
world.materials: Thin ginger slices, sugar and vinegar
world.process: Thin ginger slices are steeped in sweet vinegar, producing a crisp, sweet-sour accompaniment with ginger warmth. Fermented vinegar as an ingredient does not mean the ginger itself has undergone vegetable fermentation.
world.taste: Crisp and sweet-sour, with ginger warmth.
world.eat: Small portions served as a condiment, familiar from sushi meals.

world.name: Kawal
world.place: Western Sudan, especially Kordofan and Darfur; related traditions in Chad
world.materials: Cassia obtusifolia, also called Senna obtusifolia, leaves
world.process: Fermented leaves are dried into a dark, strongly aromatic seasoning rather than a crisp sour pickle. Not a typical lactic ferment; its specialised processing should not be treated as a home recipe.
world.taste: Strongly aromatic; a seasoning rather than a crisp, sour pickle.
world.eat: Added to onion or okra sauces and stews accompanying grain porridge.
